description.to:
The USB-C 3.2 Data Cable is a braided USB-C to USB-C cable for the USB 3 data link between a TraceCore DMA card and the analysis workstation that runs PCILeech or MemProcFS. Choose it when the cable that came with your card does not reach, when your workstation has USB-C ports, or when you want a spare on the bench.

## Key specifications

- **USB 3.2 Gen 2 rating (10 Gbps).** A Gen 2 cable also carries 5 Gbps (Gen 1) links, so it suits every USB 3 port the card works in. The TraceCore 75T's data link works in USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports, Gen 1 and Gen 2.
- **USB-C plug on both ends,** each in an aluminium shell.
- **2 m or 3 m long.** Pick the length before you add it to the cart.
- **Braided nylon jacket** over shielded conductors.

## Requirements and compatibility

- One end goes into the card's USB-C data port. The other needs a USB-C port on the workstation that carries USB 3 data: a charge-only or USB 2 port will not give you a USB 3 link. If your workstation has only USB-A ports, use a USB-C to USB-A cable instead.
- Plug straight into a USB 3 port on the motherboard's rear panel. Hubs, docks and front-panel connectors can drop the link to a lower speed.
- Use the shortest length that reaches. Signal margin at USB 3 speeds shrinks as a cable gets longer, so choose 2 m unless you need the extra metre.

## In the box

- USB-C to USB-C data cable, 2 m or 3 m as ordered
- Hook-and-loop cable tie

## Setup

Connect the card's data port as shown in [How to Install a PCIe DMA Card](/guides/install-a-pcie-dma-card), then confirm the link with the connection test and speed test in [Test a DMA Card: pcileech probe and benchmark Explained](/guides/dma-card-connection-and-speed-test).

## Questions

### Do I need this cable to use a TraceCore DMA card?

No. Each TraceCore card comes with its own cable, listed under In the box on the card's product page. This cable adds length or a USB-C to USB-C connection.

### How do I check that the link runs at USB 3 speed?

Run `pcileech benchmark` on the analysis workstation. If 16 MB reads come in below 45 MB/s, PCILeech warns that the connection is most likely running at USB 2 speed. Move the cable to a rear-panel USB 3 port, remove any hub or dock and test again. If it stays slow, work through [DMA card troubleshooting](/guides/dma-card-troubleshooting).

### Does it work with USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports?

Yes. USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 Gen 1 and Gen 2 are the same 5 Gbps and 10 Gbps signalling under different names, and a Gen 2 rated cable carries both.

description.to:
The Thermal Kit is an optional cooling upgrade for the TraceCore 75T DMA card: a finned, anodised aluminium FPGA heatsink, pre-cut thermal pads and retention clips. It is meant for cards that run sustained workloads, such as long live memory acquisitions or hours of continuous reads during research and FPGA development, and for cards fitted in cases with little airflow around the PCIe slots.

## What each part does

- **Heatsink.** The fins carry heat away from the Xilinx Artix-7 FPGA into the air moving through the case. Anodising is a hard oxide layer that protects the aluminium surface.
- **Thermal pads, 1.5 mm, 6 W/mK.** The pads fill the gap between the chip and the heatsink base. W/mK is thermal conductivity: the higher the figure, the more easily heat crosses the pad. They come pre-cut, so there is nothing to trim.
- **Retention clips.** The clips hold the heatsink in place, so fitting needs no tools and no screws.

## Requirements and compatibility

- Listed for the TraceCore 75T. Before fitting it to any other board, ask us on Discord or at {{supportEmail}}.
- A heatsink only works when air moves through the case. Check that the case fans move air past the expansion slots.
- The fins add height on the component side of the card, so check the clearance to the card in the neighbouring slot.
- Work with the computer shut down and unplugged, and handle the card by its edges after touching a grounded metal part of the case.

## In the box

- Finned aluminium heatsink
- Pre-cut thermal pads (×2)
- Retention clips

## Setup

The fitting order is: power down and remove the card, clean the chip surface, fit the pads, clip on the heatsink, then reinstall the card and run the connection test again. Step-by-step instructions are in [Install a DMA Card Heatsink and Thermal Pads](/guides/install-dma-card-thermal-kit). For removing and refitting the card itself, see [How to Install a PCIe DMA Card](/guides/install-a-pcie-dma-card).

## Questions

### Does my 75T need the Thermal Kit?

No, it is an optional upgrade. Consider it if the card runs for long periods or sits in a cramped case with little airflow.

### Do I need thermal paste as well?

No. The pre-cut pads are the thermal interface between the chip and the heatsink, so no paste is needed.

### Will it fit the TraceCore 100T Pro or other boards?

The kit is listed for the 75T only. Contact us before ordering it for another board.

description.to:
The DMA Mini PC is a compact desktop computer for use as the analysis workstation with a TraceCore DMA card. In a PCILeech setup, the DMA card sits in a PCIe slot of the target computer and passes memory reads over its USB 3 data link to a separate machine that runs PCILeech, MemProcFS and the rest of your tools. Keeping that machine separate means your tools, logs and memory images stay off the system you are examining, which is standard practice in memory forensics and incident response.

## Key specifications

- **AMD Ryzen 5 3500U.** A 4-core, 8-thread processor running at 2.1 GHz base and up to 3.7 GHz boost, with AMD Radeon Vega 8 integrated graphics (AMD specifications).
- **8 GB RAM and a 128 GB M.2 SSD.** The SSD holds the operating system, your tools and any images you save locally.
- **3 × USB 3.2 ports.** One carries the DMA card's data link; the other two are free for an external drive or other peripherals.
- **2 × HDMI display outputs** for your monitor.
- **Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac)** for network access, updates and moving results to network storage.

## Requirements and compatibility

- Connect the DMA card's data cable directly to one of the USB 3.2 ports, not through a hub or dock. A USB 2 connection still works but is far slower, and PCILeech warns when 16 MB reads fall below 45 MB/s.
- PCILeech and MemProcFS run on Windows and Linux. The PCILeech documentation reports higher FPGA throughput on Windows than on Linux.
- Use PCILeech and MemProcFS only on computers you own or are authorized to examine. Treat memory images as evidence: encrypt them, limit who can open them and record every copy to keep the chain of custody.

## In the box

- DMA Mini PC

## Setup

Start with first boot and updates in [Choosing a Forensic Analysis Workstation for an FPGA Card](/guides/choosing-an-analysis-pc). Then install the driver and software with [FT601 Driver and PCILeech Setup](/guides/ft601-driver-and-pcileech-setup), and confirm the card's link with the connection test and speed test in [Test a DMA Card: pcileech probe and benchmark Explained](/guides/dma-card-connection-and-speed-test).

## Questions

### Do I need the DMA Mini PC to use a TraceCore DMA card?

No. Any Windows or Linux computer with a free USB 3 port can be the analysis workstation. The Mini PC is a small, dedicated option that keeps analysis off your everyday computer.

### Is a DMA card included?

No. The DMA Mini PC is sold on its own, and TraceCore DMA cards are listed separately in the shop.

### Is 128 GB enough for memory images?

For small targets, yes. A full memory image is as large as the target's RAM, and the SSD also holds the operating system and tools, so plan an external drive or network storage for 32 GB or 64 GB targets.

description.to:
The TraceCore 75T is an FPGA DMA card for memory forensics, incident response, security research and FPGA development. It installs in a PCIe slot of the target system, reads that system's memory by direct memory access, and passes the data over a USB 3 link to a separate analysis workstation running tools such as PCILeech and MemProcFS. Use a DMA card only on computers you own or are authorized to examine.

## What the specs mean

- **Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A75T.** The FPGA runs the card's PCIe and USB logic. Its 75,520 logic cells are more than twice those of a 35T, which leaves room for FPGA designs of your own.
- **PCIe x1.** The card uses one PCIe lane, as PCILeech FPGA designs do, and fits x1, x4, x8 and x16 slots.
- **USB-C USB 3 data link.** The link to the analysis workstation works in USB 3.1 and USB 3.2 ports, Gen 1 and Gen 2. A USB 2 port still connects but is far slower: `pcileech benchmark` warns when 16 MB reads fall under 45 MB/s.
- **PCILeech-compatible.** The card works as a PCILeech FPGA device, with 64-bit memory access and raw PCIe TLP access. This describes the hardware interface; it is not an endorsement by the PCILeech project.
- **Kill switch.** A switch on the I/O panel, at the bracket end of the card, enables or disables the card without unplugging it.

## Requirements and compatibility

- A free PCIe slot in the target system, and the full-height or low-profile bracket that fits its case.
- An analysis workstation with a USB 3 port, ideally on the rear of the motherboard. The [DMA Mini PC](/product/dma-mini-pc) is built for that job.
- Platform protections on the target, such as an active IOMMU (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi) or Kernel DMA Protection, limit what any DMA card can read. [DMA card compatibility](/guides/dma-card-compatibility) explains how to check their status.

## In the box

- TraceCore 75T DMA card with the bracket you choose
- USB-C to USB-A data cable

Like every unit we ship, it is tested in the TraceCoreLab lab before dispatch and covered by a 3-month replacement warranty, with setup help on Discord. For long acquisitions in cases with little airflow, the [Thermal Kit](/product/thermal-kit) adds a clip-on heatsink.

## Setup

Follow [how to install a PCIe DMA card](/guides/install-a-pcie-dma-card), then the [driver and PCILeech setup guide](/guides/ft601-driver-and-pcileech-setup), and confirm the link with the [connection and speed test](/guides/dma-card-connection-and-speed-test). New to this hardware? Start with [what is a PCIe DMA card](/guides/what-is-a-pcie-dma-card).

## Common questions

### Should I choose the 75T or the 100T Pro?

For PCILeech and MemProcFS work the USB link, not the FPGA size, sets read speed, so the 75T suits most buyers. The [TraceCore 100T Pro](/product/tracecore-100t-pro) has about 34% more logic for larger designs of your own. [35T vs 75T vs 100T](/guides/artix-7-35t-vs-75t-vs-100t) compares them in detail.

### What does the kill switch do?

It enables or disables the card from the I/O panel, so the card can stay installed and cabled while it is not in use.

### Does it need software on the target computer?

No. The card works over PCIe, and PCILeech needs no drivers on the target. The software and the USB driver run on the analysis workstation.

See every [FPGA DMA card](/shop/dma) in the range.

The TraceCore 100T Pro is an FPGA DMA card built on the largest Artix-7 in the TraceCore range, the Xilinx XC7A100T. Like the [TraceCore 75T](/product/tracecore-75t), it installs in a PCIe slot of the target system and passes memory reads over USB to a separate analysis workstation running tools such as PCILeech and MemProcFS, for memory forensics, incident response and security research. The extra logic is there for FPGA development: PCIe and TLP research designs, hardware prototyping and on-chip debug cores of your own. Use a DMA card only on computers you own or are authorized to examine.

## What the specs mean

- **Xilinx Artix-7 XC7A100T.** 101,440 logic cells, about 34% more than the XC7A75T, with more block RAM and DSP slices for larger designs.
- **PCIe x1.** The card uses one PCIe lane, as PCILeech FPGA designs do, and fits x1, x4, x8 and x16 slots.
- **USB-C data link.** A USB-C port connects the card to the analysis workstation. Use a USB 3 port on the workstation, ideally on the rear of the motherboard.
- **PCILeech-compatible.** The card works as a PCILeech FPGA device. This describes the hardware interface; it is not an endorsement by the PCILeech project.
- **Kill switch.** A switch on the I/O panel, at the bracket end of the card, enables or disables the card without unplugging it.

## When the 100T Pro is the right choice

- You build and test your own FPGA designs and want headroom in logic, block RAM and DSP slices.
- You add on-chip logic analyzer cores next to a PCIe design, which use block RAM for sample buffers.
- You want one board for PCILeech-based work and for your own FPGA development.

For memory acquisition alone, read speed depends on the USB link far more than on FPGA size, so the 75T is usually enough.

## In the box

- TraceCore 100T Pro DMA card with the bracket you choose
- USB-C to USB-A data cable

Like every unit we ship, it is tested in the TraceCoreLab lab before dispatch and covered by a 3-month replacement warranty, with setup help on Discord.

## Setup

Install it with [how to install a PCIe DMA card](/guides/install-a-pcie-dma-card), set up the analysis workstation with the [driver and PCILeech setup guide](/guides/ft601-driver-and-pcileech-setup), then run the [connection and speed test](/guides/dma-card-connection-and-speed-test).

## Common questions

### Is the 100T Pro faster than the 75T?

Not for memory reads in general. Both cards use a PCIe x1 link and a USB data link, and those links set the speed. The 100T Pro's advantage is logic for your own designs; [35T vs 75T vs 100T](/guides/artix-7-35t-vs-75t-vs-100t) explains why.

### What does the kill switch do?

It enables or disables the card from the I/O panel, so the card can stay installed and cabled while it is not in use.

### Which platform protections affect it?

An active IOMMU (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi), virtualization-based security and Kernel DMA Protection all limit DMA from PCIe devices. [DMA card compatibility](/guides/dma-card-compatibility) shows how to check their status on a system.

Browse all [FPGA DMA cards](/shop/dma).

description.to:
## What the DC505 does

The DICHEN DC505 is a video fuser with built-in capture. It shows two video sources on one monitor: the main source provides the picture, and the overlay source is keyed on top, so its background drops out and only its graphics stay visible. A streamer can run alerts, lower-thirds or a chat panel from a second computer; a presenter can lay notes, a timer or a logo over slides; an AV technician can build picture-in-picture layouts or digital signage. The DC505 is built for high-refresh monitors and can record or stream the result at the same time.

## Key specs in plain words

- **HDMI 2.1 mode.** Vendor-listed up to 1080p 550 Hz, 1440p 360 Hz and 4K 160 Hz. The top modes depend on the monitor's timing; many monitors settle at 1080p 500 Hz, 1440p 320 Hz and 4K 144 Hz. With reduced-blanking timing these modes fit inside the FRL 48 Gbit/s link at 8-bit RGB.
- **DisplayPort 1.4 mode.** Vendor-listed up to 1080p 500 Hz, 1440p 320 Hz and 4K 144 Hz. DP 1.4 (HBR3) carries 25.92 Gbit/s of video uncompressed, and these modes need about 31 to 34 Gbit/s at 8-bit RGB, so they rely on Display Stream Compression (DSC) in the graphics card and monitor. Without DSC, plan on about 1440p 240 Hz or 4K 120 Hz.
- **Capture output.** 1080p 60 Hz video with audio, taken from one source directly or from the fused picture, while the overlay keeps running (vendor-listed).
- **EDID modes.** EDID is the data a monitor sends to describe the resolutions and refresh rates it supports. Adaptive uses an adapted timing, Native passes the monitor's own EDID through, and Custom uses a profile you choose. Either way, the EDID handshake offers both sources only modes that the monitor and the DC505 can carry.

## Requirements and compatibility

- **HDMI 2.1 mode:** both graphics cards and the monitor need HDMI 2.1 with FRL at 48 Gbit/s. HDMI 2.1 features are optional, so a port labelled HDMI 2.1 may not support FRL 48G; check each device's specifications. Use Ultra High Speed HDMI cables.
- **DisplayPort 1.4 mode:** DP 1.4 on both graphics cards and the monitor, with certified DP 1.4 (HBR3) cables.
- **NVIDIA RTX 50 Series:** vendor-listed as flicker-free. Some laptops with an RTX 5070 Ti or newer GPU need the 12G × 4 mode, which is HDMI 2.1 FRL at 48 Gbit/s over four 12 Gbit/s lanes.
- Before you buy, check your monitor's mode with the [pixel clock calculator](/tools/pixel-clock-calculator).

## In the box

The DC505 video fuser and its power supply. Video cables are not included.

## Setup

[DisplayPort and HDMI 2.1 fuser setup](/guides/displayport-and-hdmi-2-1-fuser-setup) covers cabling, mode selection and the capture output. If a resolution or refresh rate is missing, see [fix wrong resolution or refresh rate](/guides/video-fuser-resolution-and-refresh).

## Questions

### Do the graphics cards and the monitor all need HDMI 2.1?

For the HDMI modes, yes: every device in the chain needs HDMI 2.1 with FRL at 48 Gbit/s. If your graphics cards and monitor have DisplayPort 1.4 instead, use the DisplayPort mode.

### Why do the top DisplayPort modes need DSC?

They need more data than DP 1.4 carries uncompressed. 4K 144 Hz at 8-bit RGB needs about 31.4 Gbit/s against 25.92 Gbit/s available, so the stream has to be compressed with DSC to fit. All mode figures here are vendor-listed, not TraceCoreLab measurements.

### Can I capture while the overlay is running?

Yes. The vendor lists 1080p 60 Hz capture with audio while fusion is active, from a direct source or from the fused picture.

TraceCoreLab ships the DC505 worldwide with a 3-month replacement warranty, and setup help is available on our Discord.

description.to:
## What the D60 4K does

The DICHEN D60 4K is a DisplayPort video fuser. It shows two video sources on one monitor: the main source provides the picture, and the overlay source is keyed over it so only its graphics remain. Typical jobs are stream overlays drawn on a second computer, presentation overlays such as speaker notes or a countdown, picture-in-picture layouts, and digital signage where a ticker or clock runs over a playback feed. It suits high-refresh monitors, from 4K 120 Hz screens to 3440 × 1440 ultrawides and 3840 × 1080 super-ultrawides.

## Key specs in plain words

- **DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3).** Four lanes at 8.1 Gbit/s make the 32.4 Gbit/s figure on the spec sheet. After 8b/10b encoding, 25.92 Gbit/s is left for video, and every mode has to fit inside that.
- **4K 120 Hz in RGB.** At 8-bit colour with CVT reduced-blanking timing, 4K 120 Hz needs about 25.8 Gbit/s. It fits without compression, with almost no room to spare.
- **Vendor-listed modes.** 4K 120 Hz, 1440p 240 Hz, 1080p 360 Hz, 3440 × 1440 at 144 to 180 Hz depending on the monitor, and 3840 × 1080 at 120 Hz. At 8-bit RGB, all of them fit DP 1.4 without DSC.
- **Automatic adaptation.** The D60 matches resolution and refresh rate on its own when you connect it, so a standard setup needs no configuration.
- **Front panel.** A full-colour status display and a rotary knob.

## Requirements and compatibility

- A DisplayPort 1.4 monitor and graphics output, with certified DP 1.4 (HBR3) cables.
- For high-refresh modes, the vendor lists an HDMI 2.1 output on the overlay source.
- Monitors listed as verified: AOC CU34G3X at 3440 × 1440 and 165 Hz, and Skyworth 44C1G at 3840 × 1080 and 120 Hz.
- Your monitor's own EDID timing sets the exact pixel clock. DP 1.4 carries about 1080 MHz at 8-bit RGB and 4K 120 Hz needs about 1076 MHz, so check your mode with the [pixel clock calculator](/tools/pixel-clock-calculator).

## In the box

The D60 4K video fuser and a power supply. Cables are not included.

## Setup

Follow [DisplayPort and HDMI 2.1 fuser setup](/guides/displayport-and-hdmi-2-1-fuser-setup) to connect the D60 and check the overlay with a test pattern. For the bandwidth background, read [pixel clock and fuser bandwidth](/guides/pixel-clock-and-fuser-bandwidth).

## Questions

### Will my monitor work through the D60?

If its mode needs a pixel clock under about 1080 MHz at 8-bit RGB, it fits DP 1.4 without compression. 1440p 240 Hz needs about 1026 MHz and 3440 × 1440 at 180 Hz about 995 MHz with reduced blanking. Modes close to the limit may need a tighter timing.

### Can I use 10-bit colour at 4K 120 Hz?

Not without compression. 10-bit colour adds a quarter more data, which takes 4K 120 Hz to about 32 Gbit/s, more than DP 1.4 carries uncompressed. Use 8-bit RGB for that mode.

### What does the overlay source need?

For high-refresh modes, an HDMI 2.1 output (vendor-listed). It must also drive the same resolution and refresh rate as the main source.

TraceCoreLab ships worldwide and covers the D60 with a 3-month replacement warranty; ask on our Discord if you need help with setup.

description.to:
## What the DC1A255-H3 does

The DICHEN DC1A255-H3 is an HDMI 2.0 video fuser with three ports: two inputs for your video sources and one output to the monitor. The main source provides the picture and the overlay source is keyed over it, so a second computer can add stream graphics, a presentation timer, captions or a picture-in-picture window. It suits 1080p and 1440p high-refresh monitors, ultrawides up to 3440 × 1440 and 4K screens at 60 Hz, whether on a streaming desk, in a classroom or behind a signage display.

## Key specs in plain words

- **HDMI 2.0 bandwidth.** HDMI 2.0 runs at 18 Gbit/s, of which 14.4 Gbit/s is video data, and limits the pixel clock to 600 MHz. With reduced-blanking timing, 1080p 240 Hz needs about 583 MHz and 1440p 144 Hz about 587 MHz, which is why those are the top modes.
- **Vendor-listed modes.** 1080p up to 240 Hz, 1440p up to 144 Hz, 3440 × 1440 up to 100 Hz (listed as 3K) and 4K up to 60 Hz.
- **Native EDID passthrough.** EDID is the data that tells a graphics card which resolutions and refresh rates a monitor supports. The DC1A255 passes the monitor's own EDID to both sources automatically, so the EDID handshake offers each one the monitor's real modes.
- **Signal support.** The vendor lists DDC, HPD, CEC and HDCP over the HDMI link. The DC1A255 is plug-and-play.

## Requirements and compatibility

- HDMI outputs on both sources and an HDMI input on the monitor. For DisplayPort graphics cards, a DisplayPort fuser such as the [D60 4K](/product/d60-4k-fuser) is the simpler route.
- For 1080p 240 Hz and 1440p 144 Hz, use HDMI cables rated for 18 Gbit/s (Premium High Speed or better).
- Set both sources to the same resolution and refresh rate.
- Unusual monitor? Check its mode with the [pixel clock calculator](/tools/pixel-clock-calculator).

## In the box

The DC1A255-H3 video fuser, a power adapter and two HDMI cables.

## Setup

[HDMI video fuser setup](/guides/hdmi-video-fuser-setup) walks through cabling, the status LEDs and first power-on.

## Questions

### Why does 1440p stop at 144 Hz?

HDMI 2.0 limits the pixel clock to 600 MHz. 1440p 144 Hz uses about 587 MHz; 165 Hz would need about 680 MHz, more than the link carries.

### How many HDMI cables do I need?

Three: one from each source and one to the monitor. Two are in the box, and the monitor's own HDMI cable usually covers the third.

### Do I need to set up EDID?

No. Native EDID passthrough hands the monitor's EDID to both sources automatically. If a mode is still missing, see [fix wrong resolution or refresh rate](/guides/video-fuser-resolution-and-refresh).

The DC1A255-H3 ships worldwide from TraceCoreLab with a 3-month replacement warranty and support on Discord.

## What the Dichen Fuser does

The Dichen Fuser is an HDMI video fuser from DICHEN. It combines two HDMI sources on one monitor: the main source fills the screen and the overlay source is keyed over it, so only its graphics show. Use it to add stream overlays from a second computer, put speaker notes or a countdown over a presentation, run a picture-in-picture window, or lay a clock or ticker over a signage feed. EDID is handled automatically, which makes it an easy first video fuser for HDMI monitors.

## Key specs in plain words

- **Vendor-listed modes.** 1920 × 1080 up to 240 Hz, 2560 × 1440 up to 144 Hz, 2560 × 1080 up to 200 Hz, 3440 × 1440 up to 100 Hz and 3840 × 2160 up to 60 Hz.
- **What limits them.** These modes match what an HDMI 2.0-class link carries, about 600 MHz of pixel clock. 1080p 240 Hz needs about 583 MHz with reduced-blanking timing. 2560 × 1080 at 200 Hz needs about 628 MHz with standard reduced blanking, so it runs only on monitors whose own timing is tighter.
- **Automatic EDID.** EDID is the data a monitor sends to describe the resolutions and refresh rates it supports. The Dichen Fuser adapts it automatically, so both sources are offered modes the monitor can display without any manual setup.
- **Ultrawide and 4K.** 21:9 monitors at 2560 × 1080 and 3440 × 1440 are covered, and 4K at 60 Hz suits presentation screens and signage.

## Requirements and compatibility

- HDMI outputs on both sources and an HDMI input on the monitor.
- Set both sources to the same resolution and refresh rate before you connect them.
- For 1080p 240 Hz and 1440p 144 Hz, use HDMI cables rated for 18 Gbit/s (Premium High Speed or better).
- Check an unusual mode with the [pixel clock calculator](/tools/pixel-clock-calculator) before you buy.

## In the box

The Dichen Fuser.

## Setup

[HDMI video fuser setup](/guides/hdmi-video-fuser-setup) covers cabling, the status LEDs, the front-panel keys and automatic EDID. For a black screen, a pink tint or a wrong refresh rate, see [video fuser troubleshooting](/guides/video-fuser-troubleshooting).

## Questions

### Do I need to configure EDID?

No. Automatic EDID adaptation runs on its own. If a mode is missing, [fix wrong resolution or refresh rate](/guides/video-fuser-resolution-and-refresh) explains what to check.

### Do both sources need the same resolution?

Yes. Set both to the same resolution and refresh rate before connecting, then let the Dichen Fuser adapt.

### Will 2560 × 1080 at 200 Hz work on my monitor?

It is vendor-listed, but it depends on your monitor's timing. If the monitor's EDID gives a pixel clock above about 600 MHz for that mode, use 180 Hz, which needs about 560 MHz.

TraceCoreLab ships the Dichen Fuser worldwide with a 3-month replacement warranty and Discord support.

## What the DC1A686-D3ZC does

The DICHEN DC1A686-D3ZC is a DisplayPort 1.4 video fuser with three full-bandwidth DP ports: two inputs and one output. It keys an overlay source over the main picture on one monitor, and the two sources do not have to match: the vendor lists different resolutions on each source, with scaling. It is built for very high-refresh monitors and streaming desks, carrying stream graphics from a second computer, presentation overlays, picture-in-picture monitoring and capture for live streaming.

## Key specs in plain words

- **Vendor-listed maximums.** 1080p at 639 Hz, 1440p at 364 Hz, 3440 × 1440 at 264 Hz, 4K at 164 Hz, and 720p at 1000 Hz and above.
- **Why those modes need DSC.** DP 1.4 (HBR3) carries 25.92 Gbit/s of video uncompressed. At 8-bit RGB with reduced-blanking timing, that covers roughly 1080p 400 Hz, 1440p 250 Hz, 3440 × 1440 190 Hz or 4K 120 Hz. Every headline mode above those figures depends on Display Stream Compression (DSC) in the graphics cards and monitor; 1080p 639 Hz, for example, needs about 47 Gbit/s uncompressed.
- **Colour.** RGB or YCbCr at 8, 10 or 12 bits per channel. Deeper colour costs bandwidth: 10-bit carries 25% more data than 8-bit, and 12-bit 50% more.
- **Native EDID passthrough.** The monitor's EDID goes to both sources, so each graphics card is offered the monitor's real modes.
- **Switching and capture.** One-button switching between the two sources, and capture for live streaming at 1080p 60 Hz with audio (both vendor-listed).

## Requirements and compatibility

- DisplayPort 1.4 on both graphics cards and the monitor. For modes above the uncompressed figures, all three must support DSC.
- Three certified DP 1.4 (HBR3) cables: one from each source and one to the monitor. Cables are not in the box.
- Check your target mode with the [pixel clock calculator](/tools/pixel-clock-calculator).

## In the box

The DC1A686-D3ZC video fuser and a power supply. Pick the case colour in the product options.

## Setup

[DisplayPort and HDMI 2.1 fuser setup](/guides/displayport-and-hdmi-2-1-fuser-setup) covers cabling and model notes, and [pixel clock and fuser bandwidth](/guides/pixel-clock-and-fuser-bandwidth) explains the DSC limits in detail.

## Questions

### Do all the listed modes work over DP 1.4?

Only with DSC. Without it, plan on about 1080p 400 Hz, 1440p 250 Hz or 4K 120 Hz at 8-bit RGB. The higher figures are vendor-listed, not TraceCoreLab measurements.

### Can the two sources run different resolutions?

Yes. The vendor lists mixed-resolution operation with scaling, so the overlay source does not have to match the main source's mode.

### Which cables do I need?

Three certified DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3) cables: two for the sources and one for the monitor. Uncertified cables are a common cause of flicker or a black screen at high refresh rates.

TraceCoreLab ships the DC1A686-D3ZC worldwide with a 3-month replacement warranty; our Discord team can help with setup.

## What the GODLIKE 4K Pro does

The GODLIKE 4K Pro is a DisplayPort video fuser. It combines two video sources on one monitor: the main source provides the picture and the overlay source is keyed over it, so a second computer can add stream graphics, a presentation timer, notes or a picture-in-picture window. It suits 4K 120 Hz monitors and high-refresh 1440p and 1080p panels, and its remote control lets you change modes without reaching for the unit.

## Key specs in plain words

- **Vendor-listed modes.** 3840 × 2160 at 60 or 120 Hz; 2560 × 1440 at 144 or 240 Hz; 1920 × 1080 at 144, 165, 240 or 360 Hz; 2560 × 1080 at 165 Hz; 3440 × 1440 at 60 Hz.
- **Full 4:4:4 chroma.** Every pixel keeps its own colour information instead of sharing it with its neighbours, as 4:2:2 and 4:2:0 subsampling do. Small text and thin lines in an overlay stay sharp.
- **Bandwidth.** 4K 120 Hz at 8-bit RGB needs about 25.8 Gbit/s with reduced-blanking timing, just inside the 25.92 Gbit/s that DisplayPort 1.4 (HBR3) carries uncompressed. 1440p 240 Hz needs about 24.6 Gbit/s and 1080p 360 Hz about 22.4 Gbit/s, so the listed modes fit without DSC at 8-bit colour.
- **Switching.** It switches between the main and overlay channels; the vendor describes the switch as seamless, without a black screen or stutter.
- **Controls.** A remote control, front buttons labelled TR, RES, CH and FUSION, status LEDs for power and fusion, and RGB lighting.

## Requirements and compatibility

- Overlay source graphics (vendor-listed): AMD RX 470, NVIDIA RTX 2060 or AMD Radeon 780M integrated graphics, or newer.
- DisplayPort on both sources and the monitor. For 4K 120 Hz and 1440p 240 Hz, every device needs HBR3, which DisplayPort 1.4 provides.
- Set both sources to the same resolution and refresh rate.
- Power comes from the included 12 V, 2 A adapter with a US plug; an EU plug adapter is in the box.

## In the box

The GODLIKE 4K Pro video fusion device, a remote control, two DisplayPort cables, a 12 V 2 A power adapter with a US plug, and an EU plug adapter.

## Setup

[DisplayPort and HDMI 2.1 fuser setup](/guides/displayport-and-hdmi-2-1-fuser-setup) covers cabling and model notes. If the picture is black or tinted, see [video fuser troubleshooting](/guides/video-fuser-troubleshooting).

## Questions

### What does the overlay source need?

A graphics card at least as capable as an AMD RX 470, NVIDIA RTX 2060 or AMD Radeon 780M (vendor-listed), with a DisplayPort output that can drive the same mode as the main source.

### What does 4:4:4 chroma mean for overlays?

Colour detail is kept for every pixel, so coloured text, thin borders and small icons in the overlay look crisp rather than smeared.

### Is DisplayPort 1.4 enough for 4K 120 Hz?

Yes, at 8-bit RGB. 4K 120 Hz needs about 25.8 Gbit/s, and DP 1.4 carries 25.92 Gbit/s uncompressed. 10-bit colour at 4K 120 Hz would need about 32 Gbit/s, which needs DSC.

TraceCoreLab ships the GODLIKE 4K Pro worldwide with a 3-month replacement warranty and setup help on Discord.

description.to:
The Ferrum USB passthrough device sits between a USB mouse or keyboard and the computer it is used on, and passes the input through over high-speed USB. It suits setups where an input device has to run through an inline passthrough device without giving up its polling rate or the maker's own software, including mice set to 2000, 4000 or 8000 Hz. The housing is aluminium with a bead-blasted finish.

## What the specs mean

- **Polling rate up to 8000 Hz (vendor-listed).** Polling rate is how many times per second the computer collects new data from the mouse or keyboard. Full-speed USB works in 1 ms frames, which caps it at 1000 Hz. High-speed USB works in 125 µs microframes, which is what makes 8000 Hz possible.
- **Added latency (vendor-listed).** The maker lists an average added latency of 0.6 ms at 1000 Hz and 0.14 ms at 8000 Hz. These are the maker's figures, not TraceCoreLab measurements.
- **Full device passthrough.** According to the maker, the whole USB device is passed through, so the mouse maker's configuration software and device-specific features keep working.
- **Device type.** The device is set to pass through a mouse (the default), a keyboard, or both when they share one wireless receiver.

## Requirements and compatibility

- **Ports.** USB-C to the computer, USB-A for the mouse or keyboard, and a second USB-C for the control port.
- **Passthrough is plug-and-play.** The computer the mouse or keyboard is used on needs no driver. Use a rear motherboard USB port rather than a front-panel case port.
- **Control port.** The computer connected to the control port needs the Silicon Labs CP210x USB-to-UART driver. The device-type setting is made from that computer.

## In the box

- Ferrum USB passthrough device
- USB cables for the computer and control ports

Like every unit we ship, it is tested in the TraceCoreLab lab before dispatch and covered by a 3-month replacement warranty, with setup help on Discord.

## Setup

The [Ferrum setup guide](/guides/ferrum-setup) walks through the wiring, the CP210x driver install, the device-type setting and checking that the device appears. For more on polling, read [USB polling rate explained: 1000 Hz vs 8000 Hz](/guides/usb-polling-rate-1000hz-vs-8000hz).

## Common questions

### Does passthrough raise my mouse's polling rate?

No. The device passes through the rate the mouse is set to, up to 8000 Hz. A 1000 Hz mouse stays at 1000 Hz, and reaching 8000 Hz needs a mouse that supports it.

### Does it work with a wireless receiver?

Yes. Plug the receiver into the USB-A port. If one receiver serves both a mouse and a keyboard, set the device type to both so the two pass through together.

### How do I check that it is working?

The mouse or keyboard should work as normal on the computer it is plugged into. On the control-port computer, once the CP210x driver is installed, the device shows up in Device Manager under Ports (COM & LPT). To confirm the polling rate, use a polling-rate checker.

### Which should I choose, Ferrum USB passthrough or MAKCU?

[MAKCU](/product/makcu) costs less and passes a mouse through on full-speed USB, so it stops at 1000 Hz. Ferrum adds high-speed USB for up to 8000 Hz, keyboard passthrough and an aluminium housing. [MAKCU vs Ferrum](/guides/makcu-vs-ferrum) compares them side by side.

description.to:
MAKCU is a compact USB mouse passthrough board built on two Espressif ESP32-S3 microcontrollers. It sits between a USB mouse and the computer it is used on and passes the mouse through at up to 1000 Hz. It suits anyone who wants a low-cost inline passthrough device and does not need more than 1000 Hz, and it ships ready to use.

## What the specs mean

- **1000 Hz passthrough.** The ESP32-S3's built-in USB runs at full speed (12 Mbit/s), and a full-speed device can be polled at most once per millisecond. That sets the 1000 Hz ceiling.
- **Three USB-A ports.** The left port goes to the computer the mouse is used on, the middle port is the control port, and the right port takes the mouse.
- **CH343 control port.** The control port runs through a WCH CH343 USB-to-serial bridge chip.

## Requirements and compatibility

- **No driver for passthrough.** The computer the mouse is used on needs nothing installed.
- **CH343 driver for the control port.** On Windows 10 or 11, the computer connected to the middle port needs the WCH CH343 serial driver.
- **Cables.** If you replace a cable, a standard USB 2.0 or USB 3.0 USB-A to USB-A data cable does the job.

## In the box

- MAKCU USB passthrough board
- 2 × USB-A to USB-A cable

TraceCoreLab tests each MAKCU in our lab before dispatch. It carries a 3-month replacement warranty, and setup help is available on Discord.

## Setup

The [MAKCU setup guide](/guides/makcu-setup) covers the wiring, the CH343 driver install, checking the COM port and passthrough troubleshooting. [USB polling rate explained](/guides/usb-polling-rate-1000hz-vs-8000hz) goes deeper on why full-speed devices stop at 1000 Hz.

## Common questions

### Can I use a mouse that polls above 1000 Hz?

It will run at no more than 1000 Hz through MAKCU, and some high-rate mice and wireless receivers may not work through it at all. The mouse compatibility section of the setup guide has the details.

### How do I check that it is working?

The mouse should work as normal on the computer it is plugged into. On the control-port computer, after the CH343 driver install, MAKCU appears in Device Manager under Ports (COM & LPT) as USB-Enhanced-SERIAL CH343, with a COM number.

### Which should I choose, MAKCU or Ferrum?

Choose MAKCU for low-cost mouse passthrough up to 1000 Hz. The [Ferrum USB passthrough device](/product/ferrum) adds high-speed USB for up to 8000 Hz (vendor-listed), keyboard passthrough and an aluminium housing. [MAKCU vs Ferrum](/guides/makcu-vs-ferrum) compares the two.

USB input passthrough devices sit inline between a USB mouse or keyboard and a computer, and pass the input through. Two numbers matter when you compare them: the highest polling rate a device can pass through, and the latency it adds. The polling ceiling follows from USB speed. A full-speed USB link is polled at most once per 1 ms frame, which is 1000 Hz. High-speed USB can be polled once per 125 µs microframe, which allows 8000 Hz.

| Passes through | USB mouse | Mouse, keyboard or both on one receiver |
| Polling rate | Up to 1000 Hz | Up to 8000 Hz (vendor-listed) |
| USB speed | Full speed, 12 Mbit/s | High speed, 480 Mbit/s |
| Added latency | Not listed | 0.6 ms at 1000 Hz, 0.14 ms at 8000 Hz (vendor-listed) |
| Control-port driver | WCH CH343 | Silicon Labs CP210x |
| Build | Board with 2 × ESP32-S3, 3 × USB-A ports | Aluminium housing, USB-C and USB-A ports |

On both, passthrough is plug-and-play. Only the computer connected to the control port needs a driver, and the setup guides show how to install it and check that the device appears as a COM port.
